claim: The most common explanation for ghostwriting was that authorship was simply not discussed.
source: The most common explanation for ghostwriting was that authorship was simply not discussed (Table 4; 73% of responses from those who knew their names had been withheld).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the survey findings, with reference to Table 4.

claim: 47% of respondents have had the experience of reading a manuscript, writing a full report for their PI, and being no longer involved.
source: 47% of respondents have had the experience of "I read the manuscript, wrote a full report for my PI, and was no longer involved" (Table 2), a concerning breakdown in communication between invited reviewers and those actually writing the peer review report.
evidence: This is a direct report of survey results, with reference to Table 2.

claim: 39% of respondents think that ghostwriting occurs because some ECRs may not be comfortable asking for co-authorship.
source: Power imbalances may prevent an ECR from feeling able or willing to initiate this conversation with their PI. 39% of respondents think that ghostwriting occurs because "some ECRs may not be comfortable asking for co-authorship" (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a direct report of survey results, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: 43% of ghostwriting experiences were explained by co-authorship is for papers, not for peer review reports or intellectual contribution not deemed sufficient.
source: Ghostwriting is also driven by a cultural expectation that co-reviewers do not deserve named credit to the journal regardless of how much they contribute. 43% of ghostwriting experiences were explained by "co-authorship is for papers, not for peer review reports" or "intellectual contribution not deemed sufficient."
evidence: This is a summary statement of the survey findings.

claim: 28% of respondents surmise that ghostwriting occurs due to a belief that only the invited reviewer deserves authorship, even when others contribute ideas and/or text to the review report.
source: 28% of respondents surmise that ghostwriting occurs due to "a belief that only the invited reviewer deserves authorship, even when others contribute ideas and/or text to the review report."
evidence: This is a direct report of survey results.

claim: 83% of respondents disagree that the only person who should be named on a peer review report is the invited reviewer, regardless of who carried out the review.
source: These rationales for ghostwriting contradict community opinion about whether this should be the case, with 83% disagreeing that "the only person who should be named on a peer review report is the invited reviewer, regardless of who carried out the review" and 74% agreeing that "anyone that contributes ideas and/or text to the review report should be included as a co-author on the review."
evidence: This is a direct report of survey results.

claim: 74% of respondents agree that anyone that contributes ideas and/or text to the review report should be included as a co-author on the review.

claim: Many journals have policies that prevent invited reviewers from sharing manuscripts with anyone else and/or policies that prevent ECRs from serving as reviewers or co-reviewers without prior permission from the editor.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Transpose, 2019.

claim: 58% of respondents surmise that ghostwriting occurs because of a belief that including co-author information would demonstrate that the PI breached the confidentiality of the manuscript.

evidence: This is a direct report of survey results.

claim: 63% of respondents surmise that ghostwriting occurs because of a belief that reviews should only be done by the invited reviewer, and not by, or with assistance from, anyone else.

evidence: This is a direct report of survey results.

claim: COPE guidelines state that supervisors who wish to involve their students or junior researchers in peer review must request permission from the editor and abide by the editor's decision.
source: These policies derive from guidelines developed by the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE): "supervisors who wish to involve their students or junior researchers in peer review must request permission from the editor and abide by the editor's decision" (COPE Council, 2017).
evidence: This is a direct quote from COPE Council, 2017.

claim: In practice, invited reviewers often do not seek prior permissions, continue to involve ECR co-reviewers, and instead choose to withhold co-reviewer names upon submission.
source: Yet it seems that, in practice, invited reviewers often do not seek prior permissions, continue to involve ECR co-reviewers, and instead choose to withhold co-reviewer names upon submission.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the survey data.

claim: 39% of ghostwriters who discussed with the invited reviewer the possibility of including their name cite journal requires prior approval to share manuscript, which was not obtained or journal does not allow ECRs to review as the reason why their names were withheld.
source: Indeed, 39% of ghostwriters who discussed with the invited reviewer the possibility of including their name cite "journal requires prior approval to share manuscript, which was not obtained" or "journal does not allow ECRs to review" as the reason why their names were withheld.
evidence: This is a direct report of survey results.

claim: Current policies that require invited reviewers to gain permission prior to involving ECRs in peer review are not effective deterrents for ghostwriting.
source: Given how frequently ghostwriting occurs based on survey data, and how commonly journal policies are cited as the reason for ghostwriting, it seems that current policies that require invited reviewers to gain permission prior to involving ECRs in peer review are not effective deterrents for ghostwriting.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the survey data.

claim: 73% of respondents surmise that ghostwriting occurs because of a lack of a mechanism (such as a text box) to include co-reviewer information in the peer review report submission process.
source: 73% of respondents surmise that ghostwriting occurs because of a lack of such a mechanism.
evidence: This is a direct report of survey results.

claim: When asked to reflect on their own experiences, only 4% of ghostwriters gave lack of a mechanism as a reason for ghostwriting.
source: However, when asked to reflect on their own experiences, only 4% of ghostwriters gave this as a reason (though that might be due to a limitation in the design of this question, which did not include this answer in the drop-down menu and instead relied on respondents to write it in).
evidence: This is a direct report of survey results with a caveat about survey design.

claim: If a journal does not know who is reviewing a paper, it cannot be sure that there are no competing interests among the reviewers.
source: It is in the best interests of journals to provide mechanisms for ECR co-reviewers to be easily named (Mehmani, 2019). If a journal does not know who is reviewing a paper, it cannot be sure that there are no competing interests among the reviewers.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of not knowing reviewer identities.

claim: 82% of respondents disagree that there is no benefit in naming co-reviewers.
source: Two hypotheses for why ghostwriting is commonplace were refuted by our data. 82% of respondents disagree that there is no benefit in naming co-reviewers.
evidence: This is a direct report of survey results.

evidence: This is a direct report of survey results, with reference to Table 3.

claim: 87% of respondents disagree that ghostwriting occurs because researchers see value in withholding co-reviewer names.

evidence: This is a direct report of survey results.

claim: Editors did not rate co-reviewed reports as low quality in an ongoing experiment in co-reviewing at Elsevier journals.
source: These data align with results of an ongoing experiment in co-reviewing at the Elsevier journals, in which editors did not rate the co-reviewed reports as low quality, and more than half were considering co-reviewers to serve as invited reviewers on future manuscripts (Mehmani, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mehmani, 2019.

claim: More than half of editors in an ongoing experiment in co-reviewing at Elsevier journals were considering co-reviewers to serve as invited reviewers on future manuscripts.

claim: Reviewers who are earlier in their careers may be perceived by editors as better reviewers.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Black et al., 1998; Callaham and Tercier, 2007; and Evans et al., 1993.
